text: Mussolini founds the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento (Italian Combat Leagues) in Milan with about a hundred followers: war veterans and former shock troops, Futurist artists and ex-socialists. Its first program (June 1919) mixed nationalism with radical demands such as votes for women, an eight-hour day and a heavy tax on capital, most of which it dropped as it moved right in 1920–21. The name recalls the Roman fasces, a bundle of rods carried as a sign of authority, and gives us the word fascism.

text: In Munich the German Workers’ Party, soon renamed the National Socialist German Workers’ Party (NSDAP), announces its 25-point program. It demands a Greater Germany, the overturning of the Versailles treaty, and citizenship only for people of ‘German blood’, stating outright that no Jew can belong to the nation. Its economic points include nationalizing trusts, profit-sharing in large firms and land reform; in 1928 Hitler stated that the land point was aimed only at Jewish speculators. Historians still argue over how seriously the economic points were meant (debate 3B).
problem: Balance: The original omits the program's explicit exclusion of Jews (point 4), which is a settled fact and should be stated plainly. It also lists only one economic demand, so neither side of debate 3B gets its evidence: the 'socialist' reading relies on these points, and the 'right' reading relies on Hitler's 1928 reinterpretation and on the points being dropped in power. New facts (point 4 wording in paraphrase, profit-sharing, land reform, the 1928 clarification of point 17) are all in the GHDI program text and standard histories (Evans 2003). Add GHDI as a source.

text: Fascist squads converge on Rome. King Victor Emmanuel III declines to sign a martial-law decree that the army was ready to enforce, and appoints Mussolini prime minister of a coalition government. Historians debate why: fear of civil war, doubts about the army’s loyalty, and pressure from nationalists, business leaders and conservatives who saw Mussolini as a barrier to socialism are all cited. In form the appointment was legal; in practice it followed a threat of force and two years of squad violence against socialists, unions and local councils.
problem: Balance: The original reads as a neutral handover and does not explain why. The causes (elite choice, fear of the left, squad violence across 1920–22) are central to Paxton's 'stage three' and to the 'coup or not?' true/false card, which should not be answered with a flat 'false' (see .md, section 4). text: The Reichstag building burns. A young Dutch former Communist, Marinus van der Lubbe, is arrested at the scene and later executed. Whether van der Lubbe acted alone (Fritz Tobias, Hans Mommsen) or Nazis were involved (Benjamin Carter Hett, 2014) is still debated by historians.

text: Italy invades Ethiopia, a fellow member of the League of Nations, and takes Addis Ababa on 5 May 1936; League sanctions fail. Italian forces use chemical weapons, chiefly mustard gas dropped and sprayed from aircraft, in breach of the 1925 Geneva Protocol. Emperor Haile Selassie appeals to the League in person in June 1936; Ethiopian fighters (the Arbegnoch, or patriots) keep up resistance until British and Ethiopian forces drive Italy out in 1941. The war was popular in Italy, where the regime presented it as winning a place in the sun and avenging the defeat at Adwa (1896). Italy officially admitted using gas only in the mid-1990s.

Germany and Italy send troops, aircraft and tanks to the Nationalists; the Soviet Union supplies the Republic, and Britain and France adopt non-intervention.

text: Using the shooting of the German diplomat Ernst vom Rath in Paris by Herschel Grynszpan, a young Polish Jew whose family had just been expelled from Germany, as a pretext, the regime organizes a pogrom across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland. text: The International Military Tribunal for the Far East tries Japanese wartime leaders; seven, including Tōjō Hideki, are hanged on 23 December 1948. His dissent is still cited by Japanese nationalists and criticized by many historians.
problem: Balance: Pal's dissent is mentioned without its reasoning, which invites misreading in both directions (it is widely quoted as if Pal denied the atrocities). Hirohito's responsibility is a real debate. Sources: Pal's dissenting judgment; Bix, Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan (2000); a counter-view (e.g. Peter Wetzler or Noriko Kawamura).

text: SS officer who organized the deportation of Jews from across Europe to ghettos and killing centers. Seized in Argentina in 1960, he was tried in Jerusalem and hanged in 1962. problem: Balance: The 'banality of evil' phrase is a famous one-liner; it appears in the Arendt record but should be linked here too, with the evidence that challenged it.

text: Economist who ruled Portugal as prime minister from 1932 to 1968 and built the authoritarian, Catholic and corporatist Estado Novo. Supporters credit him with stabilizing public finances and keeping Portugal neutral in the Second World War; critics point to the PIDE political police, censorship, the Tarrafal prison camp, poverty and colonial wars in Africa from 1961. Historians debate whether his regime was fascist; in the mid-1930s he suppressed Portugal’s own fascist movement, the National Syndicalists (Blue Shirts).
